authority: Cambridge Principal Examiner Reports for Teachers, 9093 Papers 1 and 2, 9 series 2021-2025 (21 report variants per paper).
derivation_policy: Examiner-evidenced errors, restated in our words. No examiner-report wording appears in learner-facing output.
how_to_use: Every entry earns one MISCON card on the objective it attaches to (the work order names the slot). A MISCON card is a DISCRIMINATION: it states the error, the correct move, and the test that tells them apart. It does not simply restate the correct technique.
evidence_method: Counted over report sentences that record a weakness, filed by task (gen/er9093.py), matched by the pattern shown. report_variants is the spread; it does not measure prominence.

entries.learners: list the conventions of a form (headline, subheadings, paragraphs) as if naming them were the analysis
entries.test: for each convention, say what job it does for this reader; a convention with no job named has only been spotted

entries.report_theme: the role or purpose the task sets
entries.learners: write from a different point of view, or with a different purpose, from the one the task sets
entries.test: reread the task and name the speaker, the reader and the purpose before the first sentence; every paragraph should fit all three

entries.report_theme: features tied to audience and purpose
entries.learners: name the purpose and audience at the start and then analyse features without ever linking them back
entries.test: each analytical point should end by saying how the feature serves this text’s audience or purpose

entries.learners: misread a detail of the source (who did what, what a phrase refers to) and build the answer on the mistake
entries.test: check each detail you use against the sentence it comes from; if you cannot point to the words, do not use the detail

entries.learners: say that a word has “positive” or “negative” connotations and stop
entries.test: name the specific association (danger, warmth, officialdom) and what it makes the reader feel about the subject; “positive” names neither

entries.report_theme: frequency, formality and tone kept apart
entries.evidence_pattern: higher and lower|frequency lexis|orders of lexis|referred to as tone
entries.learners: treat how common a word is, how formal it is, and the tone of the text as one idea
entries.test: ask three separate questions: is the word everyday or rare? is it formal or informal? what attitude does the text take? The answers can differ

entries.learners: label sentences as simple, compound or complex and say nothing about what the structure does
entries.test: after the label, ask what the structure makes the reader notice or feel at that point; if the label could be deleted without loss, nothing was analysed

entries.report_theme: narrative and figurative terms used exactly
entries.learners: use a term loosely, such as calling any first-person account stream of consciousness, or any image personification
entries.test: check the term’s definition in the glossary against the example; if the example lacks the defining feature, use the plainer term

entries.learners: call every question rhetorical, and treat the rhetorical question as the only rhetorical device
entries.test: a rhetorical question expects no answer because the answer is assumed; if the text answers it, or the reader must, it is a real question

entries.learners: name the wrong feature, such as a simile called a metaphor or an adjective called an adverb
entries.test: test the example against the definition before naming it; a wrong label undermines the point built on it

entries.evidence_pattern: little or no comment on structure|focused solely on (structure|language)
entries.learners: leave structure out of the analysis, or say where things are without saying what the arrangement does
entries.test: a structural point names the arrangement (an opening, a shift, a return) and its effect on the reader at that moment

entries.evidence_pattern: quoting at|range of lines|lengthy quot|long quot
entries.learners: quote whole sentences, or cite a range of lines, instead of the words that carry the point
entries.test: a quotation is the right length when every word in it is one you go on to comment on

entries.report_theme: every point supported by the text
entries.evidence_pattern: few or no supporting|without (any )?(supporting )?(evidence|examples)|lacked exemplification|did not provide (specific )?(evidence|examples)|failed to provide evidence|without providing examples
entries.learners: make analytical points with no words quoted from the texts
entries.test: every point needs the words that prove it; a point you cannot quote for is an impression, not analysis

entries.evidence_pattern: general phrases|vague phrase|makes the reader|reader want|generalised
entries.learners: follow each quotation with a stock phrase (“this engages the reader”, “this creates a picture”) that could follow any quotation
entries.test: a precise comment could only be written about this quotation; if it fits any other, it says nothing about this one

entries.learners: write a string of separate observations with nothing joining them into a view of the text
entries.test: read the first sentence of each paragraph in turn; together they should state an argument about the whole text

entries.evidence_pattern: lift|quoted large|quote(d)? .{0,20}large amounts|copied|too much of the extract
entries.learners: copy phrases and sentences from the source into the directed response
entries.test: the content should come from the source; the sentences should be yours, in the register of the new form

entries.report_theme: the source reshaped for the new form
entries.evidence_pattern: summar|listing information|shape it to the requirements
entries.learners: summarise the source in order, instead of selecting from it and reshaping it for the new audience and purpose
entries.test: a directed response is organised by what its own reader needs; if its order matches the source’s paragraph by paragraph, it is a summary

entries.learners: write far more, or far less, than 150–200 words
entries.test: count before you finish: well outside the range, the response is a poorer fit to its form and purpose, and 1(b) time is lost

entries.report_theme: content kept to what the source supports
entries.learners: add material the source does not contain, until the response tells a different story
entries.test: every idea in the response should trace back to the source; new material has no source to compare against in 1(b)

entries.learners: leave out the conventions the form needs, such as a speech with no address to its audience or a letter with no salutation
entries.test: before writing, list the three conventions a reader of this form would miss if they were absent, and use them

entries.report_theme: both texts analysed, including your own
entries.learners: write mostly about the source and little or nothing about your own response
entries.test: count the quotations from each text; a comparison needs evidence from both, in roughly equal measure

entries.learners: compare what the two texts say instead of how they are written
entries.test: each comparative point should name a choice of form, structure or language in each text; “both talk about” compares content

entries.evidence_pattern: in turn|ongoing referenc|comparative requirement|limited comparison|minimal comparison|little comparison
entries.learners: discuss the source and then your own text, with no reference across between them
entries.test: every paragraph should mention both texts; a paragraph that could be cut out and read alone has stopped comparing

entries.evidence_pattern: tone unconnected|broad identification of tone|language use creates tone
entries.learners: name a tone (humorous, urgent) without pointing to the words that create it
entries.test: a tone is a result; point to the choices that produce it, or the claim cannot be checked

entries.learners: retell or summarise the text, often at length, instead of analysing it
entries.test: if a paragraph could be written by someone who had not noticed a single choice the writer made, it is summary

entries.report_theme: organised by argument, not by paragraph order
entries.learners: work through the text paragraph by paragraph, or jump around it with no line of argument
entries.test: plan by effect or purpose first; the text’s paragraph order should not be your paragraph order

entries.learners: name devices and sentence types one after another without saying what any of them does
entries.test: delete the name of the feature from your sentence; if nothing about meaning or effect is left, nothing was analysed

entries.learners: describe the style in general terms that are never proved by an example, or analyse details that never add up to a view of the whole
entries.test: the introduction should state a view of the whole text that the rest proves; a view with no proof, or proof with no view, is half an analysis

entries.report_theme: the writing analysed, not the topic
entries.evidence_pattern: distract|focused on aspects of the passage|affirmative agreement
entries.learners: respond to the topic (agree with it, explain the subject, add opinions) instead of analysing how the text is written
entries.test: every sentence of the answer should be about the writer’s choices; a sentence about the subject itself belongs to a different task

entries.evidence_pattern: under 200|fewer than 200|did not fully utilise|were short|very short|very brief
entries.learners: write far less than the space allows, so that nothing is developed
entries.test: a response well under half the limit rarely has room to develop the brief; plan three developed sections before writing

entries.evidence_pattern: required form|purely narrative|slip(ped)? into narrative|read more like|first-person narrative|narrative in terms of form
entries.learners: write in a different form from the one set, such as a story where a description or a speech was asked for
entries.test: read your opening and closing lines alone; they should tell a reader which form this is and who it is for

entries.report_theme: the role and occasion the brief sets
entries.evidence_pattern: did not address their role|did not acknowledge|launching straight|welcoming the audience|introducing the debate
entries.learners: ignore the role or the occasion the brief sets, such as a debate speech that never opens the debate
entries.test: name who is speaking, to whom, on what occasion; the first paragraph should make all three clear

entries.evidence_pattern: without elaborating|did not encourage|lacked enthusiasm|concrete reasons|token
entries.learners: miss the extra focus the prompt adds, such as persuading without reasons or encouraging without enthusiasm
entries.test: underline the prompt’s focus sentence; at the end, point to where each part of it is achieved

entries.evidence_pattern: few or no supporting|without (any )?(supporting )?(evidence|examples)|lacked exemplification|did not provide (specific )?(evidence|examples)|failed to provide evidence|without providing examples
entries.learners: write a commentary that never quotes the text it is about
entries.test: every point in a commentary needs a short quotation from your 1(a); without it the commentary is a list of intentions

entries.evidence_pattern: paraphrased|content of their piece|focused entirely on content|general commentary on the content
entries.learners: retell the content of your own piece instead of analysing its choices
entries.test: a commentary sentence names a choice and what it does for the brief; a sentence that says what happens in your text is content

entries.report_theme: form, structure and language all covered
entries.evidence_pattern: little or no comment on structure|focused solely on|solely on
entries.learners: comment on structure alone, or on language alone
entries.test: check the commentary has at least one point each on form, structure and language before it ends

entries.evidence_pattern: listed linguistic features|identif\w+ (some|a few) basic|stopped short|simple identification|without any supporting evidence
entries.learners: list the features used (“I used adjectives, metaphors and alliteration”) and stop
entries.test: a named feature needs its example and its effect on the reader; a list of feature names answers no part of the task

entries.evidence_pattern: lack(ed|ing|s)? paragraph|lacked paragraphs|minimal attempt at organisation|lack of structure|clear paragraphing
entries.learners: write without paragraphs, or break paragraphs at random
entries.test: each paragraph should have one job you can name in a few words; if you cannot name it, the break is in the wrong place

entries.learners: end abruptly, or rush the ending, so the piece stops rather than finishes
entries.test: an ending resolves or deliberately leaves open what the piece set up; a stop just runs out of words or time

entries.evidence_pattern: fewer than 400|under 600|word count|required word count|fewer than 600
entries.learners: write well short of 600 words, often because Section A took too long
entries.test: plan the time before starting: Section B carries half the paper’s marks and needs half its time

entries.evidence_pattern: narrative approach|narration was common|narrative details|describing a journey|journey|more narrative
entries.learners: let a description turn into a story told as a sequence of events
entries.test: if the paragraphs are ordered by “and then”, it is narrating; a description is ordered by what is noticed

entries.learners: pack in so many events and characters, or such unlikely ones, that the story has no credible shape
entries.test: in 600–900 words, one conflict, developed, carries a story further than several summarised

entries.learners: stack adjectives in front of nouns in place of one precise detail
entries.test: cut every adjective you could swap for another without loss; what remains should be the detail only this scene has

entries.report_theme: the effect the question asks for
entries.learners: tell a story that never creates the effect the question names (drama, suspense, mystery)
entries.test: name the effect, then point to the moments built to create it; if none were built for it, the task is only half done

entries.evidence_pattern: did not begin with|sentence provided|given sentence|opening sentence
entries.learners: leave out, or change, the sentence the question says the story must begin or end with
entries.test: copy the given sentence exactly where the question puts it, and make the story grow from it or towards it

entries.learners: use long stretches of dialogue that carry no story and are badly punctuated
entries.test: keep a line of speech only if it reveals character or moves the plot; set it out with its punctuation and a new line for each speaker

entries.evidence_pattern: one-sided|list of reasons|no consideration of opinions|balanced|counter
entries.learners: write a one-sided list of reasons that ends in a one-line conclusion
entries.test: a discursive piece gives the other side its strongest form before answering it; a list of reasons for one side is not a discussion

entries.learners: repeat the same point in new words instead of developing it
entries.test: each new paragraph should add a reason, an example or a consequence the earlier ones did not

entries.learners: narrow a broad issue to one aspect of it, such as technology alone in a question about modern life
entries.test: list the issue’s main aspects before planning; the answer should reach at least three

entries.learners: let the tone slide into ranting or blaming the reader
entries.test: read the piece as its named audience; if you would feel accused rather than persuaded, the tone has turned against the purpose

entries.report_theme: the form set, not a neighbouring one
entries.learners: write in the wrong form, such as an article with a headline and subheadings when an essay was set
entries.test: check the form word in the task before planning; an essay has no headline, an article does

entries.learners: recount the experience in the order it happened instead of judging it
entries.test: a review paragraph is ordered by a criterion, and says how well something met it; a paragraph ordered by “then” is a recount

entries.learners: list features, activities or selling points without evaluating any of them
entries.test: after each feature, ask: how good was it, compared with what, and why does that matter to the reader?

entries.learners: spend the words on minor or side details, such as the journey there or the snacks
entries.test: rank what a reader deciding whether to go most needs to know; the top items get the most words

entries.learners: offer personal likes and dislikes with no criteria and no critique
entries.test: a judgement names the standard it uses; “I liked it” names none, “the pacing held attention to the last scene” names one

entries.evidence_pattern: commas instead of full stops|commas rather than full stops|comma splice|separating sentences with commas
entries.learners: join two complete sentences with a comma
entries.test: if both sides of the comma could stand alone as sentences, a comma alone cannot join them

entries.learners: let the tense drift between past and present
entries.test: choose the tense of the telling once, and check each verb against it

entries.evidence_pattern: lose control of grammar|loss of grammatical control|long, complex sentences
entries.learners: write long complex sentences in which the grammar breaks down
entries.test: read each long sentence aloud; if you lose track of its subject before the end, split it

entries.learners: leave out capital letters for sentence openings and proper nouns, or write fragments that are not deliberate
entries.test: check every sentence opening and every name; a fragment is kept only if you can say what effect it is for

entries.learners: reach for ambitious vocabulary in a sense it does not have, or let an informal style slide into errors
entries.test: a plainer word used exactly beats an impressive one used wrongly; informal register is still accurate English

entries.learners: run speech into the narrative without its punctuation or new paragraphs
entries.test: each new speaker gets a new line; the spoken words sit inside the speech marks with their own punctuation
